title: The Giant's Causeway's 40,000 stone columns were shaped by cooling lava, not by giants
body: On the coast of County Antrim in Northern Ireland, about **40,000 interlocking basalt columns** step down into the sea. Legend says the giant Fionn mac Cumhaill built them as a road to fight a Scottish rival; geology says they formed 50 to 60 million years ago, in the Paleocene, when molten basalt flooded the area. As the thick lava cooled it contracted and cracked, much as drying mud does, and the cracks spread downward through the flow, leaving columns that are mostly hexagonal, though some have four to eight sides. The tallest stand about 12 m. The site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986 and draws around a million visitors a year.

slides.question: About how many basalt columns make up the Giant's Causeway?
slides.explanation: Approximately 40,000 interlocking columns. Most are hexagonal, but some have between four and eight sides, and the tallest are about 12 m high.

slides.caption: The size of each column was set mainly by how fast the lava cooled. Nearly a million people visited in 2019.

slides.heading: Giant's Causeway: fact or legend?

items.text: A giant built it to reach Scotland
It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site
The giant's wife disguised him as a baby

slides.explanation: In one legend, the giant Fionn mac Cumhaill's wife Sadhbh disguises him as a baby; his Scottish rival Benandonner flees and tears up the causeway behind him.
